questions.question: Which rights are considered second generation? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Interrelation between human rights, environmental policy, and sustainable development
  • • The Right to Life under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution forms the
  • foundation of this relationship. The Supreme Court has interpreted it to include
  • the right to live in a clean and healthy environment, establishing that
  • environmental protection is a basic human right.
  • • Environmental degradation directly violates fundamental human rights. Air and
  • water pollution, deforestation, and climate change threaten essential human needs
  • like food, health, and shelter, thereby undermining the dignity of life.
  • • Sustainable development connects human rights and environmental
  • policy. It promotes balanced progress where economic growth does not
  • harm ecological stability or human welfare.
  • • The Stockholm Declaration of 1972 was the first major international statement
  • linking environmental protection with human well-being. It affirmed that every
  • human being has a fundamental right to live in an environment that allows dignity
  • and quality of life.
  • • The Rio Earth Summit (1992) further integrated environmental and
  • developmental concerns. It emphasized that nations must pursue development
  • without destroying the ecological systems on which life depends.
  • Indian Constitutional provisions (Articles 48A and 51A(g)) embody these
  • principles. Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment,
  • while Article 51A(g) makes it a duty of every citizen to safeguard nature - showing
  • shared responsibility for environmental welfare.
  • • Human rights frameworks promote participation, awareness, and accountability in
  • environmental governance. They encourage citizens to play an active role in
  • decisions that affect natural resources and community health.
  • • The Right to Information Act (2005) and National Green Tribunal Act
  • (2010) reinforce environmental accountability. These laws empower
  • citizens to seek transparency and challenge violations affecting public
  • health and ecology.
  • • Environmental protection upholds equality and justice. It safeguards marginalized
  • and poor communities who suffer most from pollution, displacement, and resource
  • exploitation.
  • • Media and NGOs act as social catalysts for awareness, advocacy, and
  • monitoring of environmental issues. They connect civil society and the
  • government, ensuring
  • people’s voices are heard.
  • • Sustainable development ensures intergenerational equity. It preserves natural
  • resources for future generations, ensuring long-term human survival and well-
  • being.
  • The interconnection between human rights, environmental policy, and sustainable
  • development reflects a holistic approach to justice and life. Protecting the environment
  • safeguards the right to life, while sustainable development ensures that progress today does
  • not endanger tomorrow. Thus, human rights and environmental protection are not separate
  • goals - they are two sides of the same moral and constitutional vision of harmony between
  • people and planet.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is the purpose of World Heritage Sites? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Historical development of human rights (Magna Carta to UDHR)
  • • The idea of human rights evolved gradually through centuries, shaped by struggles
  • for justice, freedom, and equality. It began as privileges granted to a few but grew
  • into universal principles recognizing the dignity of all people.
  • • The Magna Carta (1215) was the first landmark in this evolution. Signed by
  • King John of England, it limited the arbitrary powers of the monarchy and
  • protected individuals against unlawful imprisonment and taxation - the earliest
  • foundation of rule of law and personal liberty.
  • • The Petition of Right (1628) further developed these principles. It declared that
  • the king could not impose taxes or imprison citizens without Parliament’s
  • consent, reinforcing that government authority must be subject to law.
  • • The English Bill of Rights (1689) strengthened parliamentary democracy. It
  • guaranteed freedoms such as free elections, speech in Parliament, and protection
  • from cruel punishments, laying the foundation of constitutional governance.
  • • The U.S. Declaration of Independence (1776) marked a turning point in
  • political philosophy. It proclaimed that all men are created equal and endowed
  • with unalienable rights - life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness -
  • emphasizing natural and inborn rights.
  • • The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789)
  • expanded these ideals into Europe. It proclaimed liberty, equality, and
  • fraternity as universal rights, asserting that sovereignty resides with the
  • people, not with rulers.
  • • The 19th century witnessed major social transformations, including the
  • abolition of slavery, recognition of workers’ rights, and early movements for
  • women’s suffrage. These struggles extended human rights beyond political
  • freedoms to social and economic justice.
  • • After World War I, the League of Nations (1919) was created to promote
  • collective security and prevent wars. Though limited in power, it introduced the
  • idea that international institutions could safeguard peace and human rights
  • across nations.
  • • The United Nations Charter (1945), drafted after the horrors of World War II,
  • reaffirmed faith in fundamental human rights, dignity, and equality. It recognized
  • that peace and human rights are interdependent and must be promoted together.
  • • The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) of 1948 became the
  • first comprehensive statement of global human rights. Adopted by the United
  • Nations General Assembly, it laid down 30 articles guaranteeing civil,
  • political, social, cultural, and economic rights to all people, regardless of
  • nation, race, or creed.
  • • The UDHR inspired legally binding covenants - ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) -
  • which together form the International Bill of Human Rights. These documents
  • institutionalized human rights as universal standards for nations and
  • governments
  • • In conclusion, the historical evolution from the Magna Carta (1215) to the
  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) signifies a profound
  • transformation in the moral and political consciousness of humanity.
  • It marks the gradual shift from exclusive privileges enjoyed by the ruling elite to
  • the universal affirmation of human dignity, equality, and liberty as inherent and
  • inalienable rights of every individual. This progression embodies the enduring
  • pursuit of justice, the consolidation of democratic ideals, and the collective
  • aspiration for global peace and human solidarity.

questions.solution_html:
• Role of CRC in advancing global child rights
  • • Adopted by UN in 1989; ratified by nearly all nations.
  • • Ensures right to survival, protection, development, and participation.
  • • Legally binds states to protect children up to 18 years.
  • • Promotes education, healthcare, and protection from exploitation.
  • • Establishes UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.
  • • Influences national laws (e.g., JJ Act, POCSO in India).
  • • Introduced Optional Protocols on child soldiers and exploitation.
  • • Promotes child participation in policy decisions.
  • • Monitors periodic state reports for compliance.
  • • Strengthened the global framework for child welfare and dignity.
